title: Micronet 800
text:
### Directories and guides

Micronet 800 had an AZ online index, published a directory in its Log On print magazine,[1] and distributed a guide for users containing a London Tube-style map of the database.[2]

### Chatlines

A form of chat room, Chatlines began in late 1984 as a single online chat service where users could post messages that other users could read and respond to. It was described in the vocabulary of the time as a "Citizens' Band (CB) emulator".[3] A year later, Chatlines was divided into six special-interest sections and moved to a mainframe computer.[4]

By 1986, eight Chatlines were available: two so-called "Daisychats", each composed of a continuous loop of linked videotex frames where, once full, the newest posting overwrote the oldest; and six online forums, where postings were archived. The forums, known as "lines", included ones for politics and religion (the latter was monitored), "Gay Chatline", and a weekly "Celebrity Chatline" (launched in 1985),[5] which operated like a phone-inusers posted questions to a celebrity, who would answer them during an interview by a Micronet editor.[6]

In June 1990, British Telecom suspended Chatlines.[7] Micronet stated that sporadic monitoring had not prevented abuse of the service, and that it would investigate how to operate Chatlines in a "fully monitored" way in future, though without committing to a reinstatement.[8] In the event, Chatlines did not return. A year later, Micronet introduced a moderated "Line Noise" forum.[9]

### Teleconferencing

DialTalk (briefly "TeleTalk"), a teleconferencing service, opened in 1988. A user could hold live conferences or discussions with up to sixty-three other users in one of 30 "rooms", and convene breakaway or private meetings in other vacant rooms.[10]

### Downloadable software

In return for a fee or royalties, Micronet 800 encouraged individuals, amateur computer groups and software companies to supply programs that could be stored on Micronet's 800 telesoftware database and downloaded by subscribers.[11]

Originally, about half of the programs were free, with the rest available at discounts of around 15% or more.[10] In early 1989, however, Micronet abandoned paid-for telesoftware and began supplying programs free of charge via a Prestel gateway.[12] Microcomputers for which programs were made available included the Amiga, Amstrad CPC, BBC Micro, IBM PC, and Spectrum.[13]

When Micronet 800 launched in 1983, providers of programs on Prestel were using a protocol drawn up by the UK's Council for Educational Technology (CET)[14,15] after consulting British Telecom, microcomputer manufacturers, users, and educational software agencies.[16] In early 1991, Micronet issued FCET, a revised version of the CET format, that much decreased download times.[17]

Micro Arts, creators of computer art in text and graphic form,[18] published articles and downloadable programs on Micronet 800 from 1985 onwards.[19]

### Games

The longest-running online game on Micronet 800 was Starnet, a turn-based game, with players sending in moves that would be executed once a day.[20] Micronet 800 also hosted Shades, one of the first real-time multiplayer games.[21] Other multiplayer games offered included The Round Britain Yacht Race,[22] Trash ("The game puts you in the role of a pan-dimensional dustman"), and Casino, which featured simulations of slot machines and games such as roulette, blackjack, keno, baccarat, and poker.[23]

### Email

Each Prestel user had a unique Mailbox numberusually derived from the last nine digits of their phone numberthat was used to address and send messages to others on Prestel. Reportedly, Micronet 800 subscribers were particularly enthusiastic about the medium, sending twice as many Mailbox messages as regular Prestel users.[24]

In 1984, Mailbox was connected to the telex system via Prestel's Telex Link: telexes could be sent and received like standard messages.[25] From mid-1987, Micronet's "Interlink" facility offered subscribers direct access to the Telecom Gold email, chat, and information service.[26,27]

### Magazines

Micronet created separate online magazines"micromags" for owners of a range of popular home computers, adapting its offering according to levels of ownership of particular models[28] and market developments.[10]

Bizznet, the first non-microcomputer section in Micronet's database, launched in 1986 with guidance for small businesses on accounting, law, tax, insurance, and finance.[29] In 1988, it was renamed Money Xtra[30] and refocused on personal finance,[31] providing consumer, financial, and tax advice, together with a legal advisory service.[32]

Xtra!, described as a leisure magazine, also began in 1986, and contained music reviews, analysis of current affairs, restaurant and bar reviews, and letters from users.[33] Separate sections covered TV and radio (Waveguide),[34] and consumer electronics (Voltage).

Computers, music, and MIDI-music were the subject of MidiSpot,[35] which incorporated Micronet's earlier Music City magazine, launched in 1988.[36]

### Gallery

This was an area of the database where, for a fee, users could rent pages and publish anything they wished, subject to monitoring by Micronet for instances of libel or obscenity.[37]
